strengths: The paper addresses an important and fundamental problem in machine learning: estimating the Bayes error rate to understand the limits of model performance and detect test-set overfitting.

The theoretical improvement on the hard-label-based estimator's bias (Theorem 1, Corollary 1, Corollary 2) is clean and substantial. It removes an unnatural dependence on the sample size n present in prior work (Ishida et al., 2023) and demonstrates an adaptive decay rate of up to O(1/m) for well-separated distributions.
The conceptual distinction between general calibration and consistent Bayes error estimation (Example 2) is very clear and provides valuable intuition for why arbitrary calibration methods can fail.

The formulation and theoretical analysis of isotonic calibration for corrupted soft labels (Theorem 2 and Theorem 3) are mathematically rigorous, leveraging non-trivial tools from shape-restricted nonparametric regression.
The paper is well-written, clearly organized, and accompanied by comprehensive proofs and empirical validations on synthetic and real-world benchmarks.
weaknesses: The method requires having a paired true hard label y_i for each instance x_i to perform the calibration step on the corrupted soft labels. In scenarios where a fully labeled set is available, the necessity of having corrupted soft labels in addition to hard labels—versus standard classification/estimation approaches—could be more clearly motivated.

The study is restricted strictly to binary classification. In many real-world applications and benchmarks (e.g., full CIFAR-10), multi-class classification is the primary setting, and binarizing multi-class tasks somewhat limits the direct applicability of the current results.

Evaluation on real-world datasets is inherently limited because the ground-truth Bayes error is unknown. While comparing against deep neural network test errors provides an upper-bound check, additional quantitative validation on high-dimensional semi-synthetic data with known ground-truth posteriors would strengthen the empirical claims.

In Theorem 3, the asymptotic error bound retains a constant factor proportional to the noise standard deviation sigma, which does not vanish as n -> inf unless the number of hard labels m per instance also increases.

strengths: Meaningful theoretical refinement over previous work: The paper sharpens the bias bounds of the hard-label-based Bayes error estimator from Ishida et al. (ICLR 2023) by removing the unnatural dependence on the sample size n and demonstrating adaptivity to margin/separation conditions (yielding an O(1/m) decay rate under clean separation rather than O(1/sqrt(m))).

Principled framework for corrupted soft labels: Tackling distorted/corrupted soft labels is practically motivated by human annotation subjectivity and LLM-generated confidences. The paper formalizes when calibration works, proves that general calibration can fail catastrophically (Example 2), and identifies order preservation as a sufficient condition for consistency via isotonic regression.

Rigorous theoretical analysis: The derivation of the non-asymptotic risk bound for binary isotonic regression (Proposition 2) via localized width and metric entropy is technically sound, and the resulting consistency rates for both noiseless (Theorem 2) and noisy (Theorem 3) monotone distortions are clearly established.

Well-structured presentation and thorough empirical validation: The synthetic simulations nicely confirm the theoretical bias decay slopes, and the real-data experiments on binarized CIFAR-10H and Fashion-MNIST-H demonstrate practical relevance where raw soft labels severely overestimate the Bayes error.
weaknesses: Restriction to binary classification: Modern classification tasks and benchmarks are predominantly multi-class. Because isotonic regression relies heavily on 1D total ordering, the proposed calibration-based approach does not trivially generalize to multi-class settings, necessitating artificial binarization of datasets like CIFAR-10 and Fashion-MNIST.

Practicality of the data collection assumptions in Section 3: The proposed corrupted soft-label estimation assumes access to pairs of corrupted soft labels and single true hard labels (\tilde{\eta}_i, y_i) for all n points. While the instance-free aspect is appealing for privacy, having calibrated access to true ground-truth labels y_i alongside corrupted confidence scores \tilde{\eta}_i in real-world pipelines warrants a clearer discussion of realistic operational scenarios.

Relatively slow statistical rate: The convergence rate with respect to n in Theorem 2 is O(n^{-1/3}), reflecting the non-parametric nature of isotonic regression. While minimax optimal for shape-constrained 1D regression, this can require relatively large sample sizes n to achieve high estimation precision.

strengths: Significantly advances the theoretical understanding of soft-label-based Bayes error estimation by improving the bias bound of the hard-label estimator from Ishida et al. (2023), eliminating the unnatural dependence on the sample size n, and demonstrating adaptive convergence rates (O(1/m) for well-separated distributions versus O(1/\sqrt{m}) in the worst case).
Provides a insightful critique of naive calibration in Bayes error estimation through Example 2, illustrating that standard calibration criteria alone do not suffice to recover the true Bayes error.

Derives rigorous non-asymptotic statistical guarantees for isotonic calibration under monotonic distortions (Theorem 2) and with additive noise (Theorem 3), supported by a new high-probability risk bound for binary isotonic regression with bounded domain (Proposition 2).
The paper is very well-written, logically structured, and clearly positions its contributions relative to prior work.

Experiments thoroughly validate both the theoretical decay rates of the bias on synthetic setups and demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed calibration method on CIFAR-10H and Fashion-MNIST-H, successfully resolving the overestimation issue observed in previous literature.
weaknesses: The proposed calibration procedure assumes access to a hard label y_i for each instance alongside the corrupted soft label \tilde{\eta}_i; while a single hard label per instance is insufficient on its own for the Ishida et al. plug-in estimator, requiring paired true hard labels for calibration is a specific setting whose practical constraints could be discussed in greater detail.

The theoretical guarantees rely heavily on the assumption that corruption is monotonic (\tilde{\eta} = f(\eta)), which may not fully capture complex, instance-dependent biases in real-world human or LLM annotations.
The scope of the paper is strictly limited to binary classification; extending these isotonic calibration guarantees and bounds to multi-class settings remains an open and non-trivial challenge.
The convergence rate under isotonic calibration is O(n^{-1/3}), which is standard for one-dimensional shape-constrained regression but slower than standard parametric rates.

strengths: The paper addresses a fundamental and practically relevant problem: estimating the Bayes error in binary classification when only approximate or corrupted soft labels are available.

The theoretical contributions are significant and rigorous: (1) it sharpens the existing bias bound of the hard-label estimator by Ishida et al. (2023), eliminating the counterintuitive dependence on sample size $n$ and showing that the bias decays at an adaptive fast rate $O(1/m)$ for well-separated distributions; (2) it formalizes the problem of corrupted soft labels and proves statistical consistency and an $O(n^{-1/3})$ convergence rate for isotonic calibration when the corruption is monotonic (with and without additive noise).

The paper provides an insightful counterexample and discussion showing that calibration alone is insufficient for accurate Bayes error estimation, thereby justifying why specific shape-constrained nonparametric methods like isotonic regression are necessary.

Extensive empirical evaluations are conducted across synthetic datasets, computer vision benchmarks (CIFAR-10H, Fashion-MNIST-H), NLP datasets (ChaosNLI), and a newly curated ICLR peer-review dataset. The use of the FeeBee evaluation framework provides objective and standardized validation showing the clear superiority of isotonic calibration over competing calibrators.
weaknesses: The scope of the theory and methods is strictly limited to binary classification. While extending to multi-class classification is noted as future work, multi-class Bayes error estimation is crucial for many practical benchmarks.

The proposed method requires access to a single ground-truth hard label $y_i \sim P(y|x_i)$ alongside each corrupted soft label $\tilde{\eta}_i$ to perform recalibration. While requiring $m=1$ true hard label is much less demanding than repeated annotations, in some real-world situations with labeling shift or subjectivity, obtaining unbiased ground-truth labels from the target distribution can still be challenging.

The convergence rate under isotonic calibration is $O(n^{-1/3})$, which is inherently slower than the standard parametric rate $O(n^{-1/2})$ due to the non-parametric nature of isotonic regression, though this appears to be the minimax optimal rate for this class of estimators.

strengths: The theoretical contributions are rigorous, elegant, and address significant limitations of prior work (Ishida et al., 2023). In particular, eliminating the unnatural dependence on the sample size n in the bias bound of the hard-label-based estimator and establishing adaptive fast rates of O(1/m) for well-separated distributions are valuable insights.

The derivation of a practically computable bias bound (Corollary 2) that depends only on a known upper bound of the Bayes error (such as the error rate of a current SOTA classifier) makes the theoretical bounds readily applicable to real-world datasets.

Formulating Bayes error estimation under corrupted soft labels and proving statistical consistency using isotonic calibration is novel and well-justified. The mathematical machinery developed (extending sharp oracle inequalities and bracketing entropy for bounded isotonic regression) is technically sound.

The empirical evaluation is comprehensive, covering synthetic benchmarks, established image datasets (CIFAR-10H, Fashion-MNIST-H), NLP datasets (ChaosNLI), and a novel real-world application to ICLR peer-review decisions. The use of the FeeBee framework provides an objective and principled evaluation on real-world datasets without ground-truth Bayes errors.

The paper is exceptionally well-written, clearly organized, and provides detailed appendices including full proofs and extensive ablation studies (such as the impact of order breakage and corruption parameter variations).
weaknesses: The method is currently restricted to binary classification. While multiclass extensions exist in related literature (e.g., Jeong et al., 2023), isotonic calibration and thresholding min{η, 1-η} do not trivially generalize to the simplex without additional structural assumptions.

The theoretical guarantees in Section 3 require the corrupted soft labels to follow an order-preserving transformation (or an order-preserving transformation with bounded additive noise and strictly positive derivative). While Appendix D.5 provides useful empirical sensitivity analysis with varying Kendall's tau, theoretical bounds under partial order violations remain an open question.

The calibration phase requires access to unbiased hard labels y_i drawn from the true posterior P(y|x_i) for the same instances. In some practical settings where corrupted soft labels are sourced (e.g., historical LLM outputs or legacy soft annotations), collecting corresponding ground-truth hard labels from the target distribution might pose an additional annotation burden.

strengths: Clear resolution of theoretical gaps in prior work: The paper significantly tightens the bias bounds of the hard-label plug-in Bayes error estimator from Ishida et al. (ICLR 2023). It removes the unnatural dependence on the sample size $n$ and demonstrates an adaptive decay rate that accelerates from $O(1/\sqrt{m})$ to $O(1/m)$ when the classes are well-separated.

Derivation of practically computable bounds: Corollary 2 provides an explicit, computable lower bound on the bias that relies solely on an upper bound of the Bayes error (such as a trained SOTA model's test error), which is shown to be over 200 times tighter than existing bounds on benchmark datasets like CIFAR-10.

Sound theoretical framework for corrupted soft labels: The paper addresses a major practical shortcoming of soft-label estimators—namely, that soft labels are often distorted or uncalibrated. By framing recalibration via binary isotonic regression, the authors establish finite-sample consistency guarantees (Theorems 2 and 3) under mild nonparametric monotonicity assumptions, supported by sharp oracle inequalities in the appendix.

Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The proposed framework is thoroughly evaluated across synthetic data, vision benchmarks (CIFAR-10, Fashion-MNIST), natural language inference (ChaosNLI), and a newly curated ICLR peer-review dataset. The paper rigorously benchmarks different calibration techniques using the FeeBee evaluation protocol, showing consistent superior performance of isotonic calibration.

High clarity and excellent technical depth: The manuscript is well-written, clearly positioned relative to prior literature, and supplemented with extensive proofs, sensitivity analyses (e.g., violations of monotonicity and derivative assumptions in Appendix D), and ablation studies.
weaknesses: Restriction to binary classification: While the theoretical analysis is deep, the current formulation is strictly confined to binary classification problems. Although multi-class classification is noted as future work, extending these bounds and calibration guarantees to multi-class settings (e.g., building on Jeong et al., 2023) would broaden the practical applicability.

Requirement of hard labels for recalibration: In the corrupted soft label setting, the method requires a paired ground-truth hard label $y_i$ for each instance to perform isotonic regression. While the instance-free aspect (not requiring $x_i$) is advantageous for privacy and circumventing the curse of dimensionality, acquiring a hard label for every sample can be restrictive in some annotation pipelines.

Convergence rate limitation: Due to the nonparametric nature of isotonic regression, the high-probability convergence bound scales as $O(n^{-1/3})$ with respect to the sample size $n$. While minimax optimal for isotonic regression, this rate is comparatively slow relative to standard parametric rates.
